members.unit:
# padd — the gamepad, as an intent client.
#
# Install to /etc/systemd/system/padd.service.
#
# Why this is a unit at all. Driving used to mean: ssh to the board, be a member of two groups
# (having logged out and back in since), and run a binary by its full path — which died with the ssh
# session. So the pad worked when someone had done all of that, and the failures were invisible in
# three separate places. Now pairing a pad (`robotctl pad pair`) is the only step, and this runs from
# boot waiting for one.
#
# It is safe to have running with no pad, which is what makes an always-on unit the simple answer
# rather than udev rules or device-unit binding: `padd` sends *nothing* when it sees no pad, and
# robotd's deadman holds the robot on its own. A pad that connects is picked up within a tick.
#
# Nothing moves on connection either — the policy is off until someone presses Start. What a paired
# pad grants is the authority to enable it, and *pairing* is the gate on that: it takes a pad held in
# pairing mode next to the robot, and `robotctl pad forget` revokes it.

[Unit]
Description=Robot gamepad intent client
Documentation=file:///opt/robot/daemon/current/docs/architecture.md

# `After`, not `Requires`: robotd is where the intents go, so starting before it is pointless — but
# a robotd that is down must not keep this unit from being started. If the socket is not there yet
# `padd` exits and systemd retries in five seconds, which is how it catches up on a slow boot.
#
# No `Wants=robotd.service` either. robotd is started at boot by its own `WantedBy=`, so all
# `Wants=` added was to start robotd again every time this unit started — and with
# `Restart=always`, a `systemctl stop robotd` came undone five seconds later whenever a pad was
# connected, because only then does `padd` write to the dead socket and exit. Stopped means stopped.
After=robotd.service local-fs.target

# The pad arrives over Bluetooth, and on this board hci0 does not exist until roughly 73 seconds
# after power-on. Ordering after bluetooth.service is nowhere near sufficient for that and is not
# meant to be: `padd` polls for a pad forever, so the radio can appear whenever it likes.
After=bluetooth.service

[Service]
Type=exec
ExecStart=/opt/robot/daemon/current/bin/padd

# Unprivileged, and this one is not a hardening choice — it is the point of the process. `padd` has
# no privileged access to the robot, which is what makes it an honest exercise of the intent API
# every day (see the crate docs). Its access is two groups and nothing else:
#
#   input  — /dev/input/event*, which is root:input 0660. Without it padd sees no pad and says so.
#   robot  — robotd's 0660 socket, the same way btd and the SDK reach it.
#
# The user and group must exist or the unit fails to start; see sysusers.d/padd.conf, installed
# alongside.
User=padd
Group=padd
SupplementaryGroups=input robot

# Restart=always, not on-failure: `padd` exits cleanly when robotd's socket is not there, and that
# is a state to retry rather than one to stay down in. Five seconds because the thing being waited
# for is a boot finishing or a daemon restarting, neither of which is helped by spinning.
Restart=always
RestartSec=5s

# Hardening, as far as a process that reads an input device can go.
#
# NOT PrivateDevices=yes: that hides /dev/input, which is the one thing this process exists to read.
# The device nodes it may open are still limited by the `input` group.
#
# AF_NETLINK is load-bearing and easy to miss: gilrs enumerates and *watches* devices through
# libudev, which is a netlink socket. Without it a pad connected after startup is never noticed,
# which presents as "the pad works only if it was on before the robot booted".
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
ProtectKernelTunables=yes
ProtectKernelModules=yes
ProtectControlGroups=yes
RestrictSUIDSGID=yes
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX AF_NETLINK
RestrictNamespaces=yes
LockPersonality=yes
MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes
SystemCallFilter=@system-service
SystemCallErrorNumber=EPERM
CapabilityBoundingSet=

# stderr → journal; level via RUST_LOG. `padd` logs at `warn` when it starts driving, when the
# policy is toggled and when a pad appears or goes away — the events someone reads the journal to
# find — and nothing per tick.
Environment=RUST_LOG=info
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal

# /run/padd/, which holds two things: identity.json — what this daemon is running, read by
# `robotctl health` and by updaterd's startup check — and pad.sock, the read-only raw input tap
# `robotctl monitor` shows the pad's own event stream from (`src/tap.rs`).
#
# `RuntimeDirectory=` rather than a path this unit is granted: it is the only mechanism that both
# creates the directory owned by this unit's User= *and* survives ProtectSystem=strict, which
# otherwise leaves the whole filesystem read-only. systemd also removes it when the unit stops, so a
# stopped daemon cannot leave behind an identity claiming to be running — nor a socket nothing is
# listening on, which is the difference between "padd is not running" and a client hanging.
#
# The tap's socket is 0660 and handed to the `robot` group by `padd` itself, so it reaches exactly
# who may already drive the robot. That is done in code rather than with `Group=robot` here, the way
# robotd does it: this process keeps its own primary group, and reaches the robot group as a
# supplementary one.
RuntimeDirectory=padd

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
